Title: "Cognitive contributors to resilience in youth from underserved populations: A brief report"
Affiliation_Corr_Author: "The protective factors (i.e. individual skills, relationship with caregivers and contextual factors) promoting resilience were correlated with cognitive factors. Further analyses yielded gender differences in these relations. Long-held beliefs that intelligence is positively associated with resilience are brought into question by these findings."
Research_Aim: "identify cognitive factors (e.g., executive functions and intelligence) promoting resilience in youth in an underprivileged population."
Research_Results: "The protective factors (i.e. individual skills, relationship with caregivers and contextual factors) promoting resilience were correlated with cognitive factors. Further analyses yielded gender differences in these relations."
Population_Characteristics: "...who live with poverty, family dysfunction, and multiple traumas participated in the study. Youth with pre-existing diagnoses of serious neurological disorder or intellectual disability (IQo70) were excluded because of inability to complete the study tasks."
Specific_ACEs: poverty; family dysfunction; multiple traumas; natural disaster; disaster/serious accident; physical abuse; sexual abuse; witnessing domestic violence; community violence; familial separation; family's serious illness
Specific_ACEs_Instruments: UCLA PTSD Reaction Index Trauma Exposure Screen [PTSDRI] (Pynoos et al., 1998)
EF_Evaluated: Working memory; Inhibitory control; Intelligence; Processing speed
EF_Instrument: Keep Track Task [KTT] (Miyake et al 2000) (working memory); Wechsler Abbreviated Intelligence Scale [WASI] (Psychological Corporation 1999); The Flanker Task [FL] (Eriksen and Eriksen 1974) (baseline reaction time; resistance to distraction); Symbol Digit Modalities Test [SDMT] (Smith 1982) (complex processing speed)
Justification_Resilience_conceptualizati: "resilience is a multi-component construct that feeds on several resources: the capacity of the individual to discover or recognize resources crucial for maintaining well-being, the capacity of the individual’s surroundings to provide those resources; and the capacity of the individual, his family and community to agree on how to share and utilize those resources (Ungar et al., 2008). ........ Resilient outcomes"
Resilience_Instrument: Child and Youth Resilience Measure [CYRM-28] (Ungar and Liebenberg, 2009)
Comments_Relation_ACEs_EF_Resilience: "ACEs and EF: Processing speed was marginally related to the CYRM-28 only for male participants. EF and resilience: Correlational analyses indicated that intelligence scores were negatively correlated with the Relationship with Caregivers subscale and marginally, and again, negatively, correlated with the Contextual Factors. Processing speed, as measured by reaction time in the neutral condition of the Flanker Task was marginally associated with the Relationship with Caregivers subscale. Female participants’ intelligence scores were negatively correlated with the subscale of Individual Skills whereas males’ intelligence scores were negatively related to the Contextual Factors subscale. Similarly, working memory as measured with the Keep Track Task was correlated with with the Individual Skills scale only for male participants, albeit marginally."

Ethics_University: University of Maryland School of Medicine
Affiliation_Corr_Author: "Department of Pediatrics, University of Maryland School of Medicine, Baltimore, MD 21201"
Research_Aim: "Examine resilience in high-risk preschoolers, and to probe contributors to their adaptive functioning."
Research_Results: "Forty-eight percent of the sample appeared resilient. Justification_Resilience_conceptualizati: "In this article, we refer to broad, successful adaptation as “resilience” and to positive functioning in a specific domain or age as “competency.” Variation in resilience is associated with several influences, such as differing early life adversities, childhood temperament and personality, and the social capital available in the home and community. It is also associated with family poverty. / The development of resilience."
Resilience_Instrument: Child Behavior Checklist [CBCL] (Achenbach, 1991); Battelle Developmental Inventory Screening Test [BDIST] (Newborg, 1984); Vineland Screener (Sparrow et al., 1993); Loneliness and Social Dissatisfaction Questionnaire (Cassidy & Asher, 1992); Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence-Revised [WPPSI-R] (Wechsler, 1989)
Comments_Relation_ACEs_EF_Resilience: "El efecto de la conectividad cerebral depende del contexto económico, especialmente en la relación entre el control ejecutivo y el procesamiento interno. Por lo que, el cerebro de los participantes se adapta de diferentes maneras en diferentes niveles socioeconómicos. Ligado a esto, los niños que viven sobre la línea de pobreza se adaptan de mejor manera a los diferentes contextos(resiliencia), a diferencia de los que viven bajo la línea de pobreza." "We found that there is not a universally strong link between performance on tests of executive functioning and these more real-world outcome measures. We found that cognitive test scores were more highly correlated with academic performance in children above than below poverty. The lower correlation for children below poverty likely reflects obstacles that hinder their ability to reach their full potential, such as fewer school resources and lower quality of instruction."

Title: "A qualitative analysis of factor impacting resilience among youth in post‑conflict Liberia"
Journal: Child and Adolescent Psychiatry and Mental Health
Affiliation_Corr_Author: "The Chester M. Pierce, MD Division of Global Psychiatry, Massachusetts General Hospital, 5 Longfellow Place, Boston, MA 02114, USA; Harvard Medical School, 25 Shattuck St., Boston, MA 02115, USA; University of Illinois College of Medicine, 1853 West Polk St, Chicago, IL 60612, USA."
Research_Aim: "Identify factors contributing to resilience among youth in post-conflict Liberia."
Research_Results: "Youth enrolled in school demonstrated greater adaptive functioning. This was particularly true for boys in any school setting and girls attending private school. Youth not attending school were more likely to have lost family members or become estranged from them, and many were also engaging in substance use. /// Emotion regulation, cognitive flexibility, agency, social intelligence and, in some cases, meaning-making were found in participants who showed resilient outcomes."
Population_Characteristics: 35 public school students; 11 private school students; 29 children not attending school at the time of the interviews
Specific_ACEs: exposure to war-related violence; pandemic (Ebola); parents' death; displacement; poverty; substance abuse
EF_Evaluated: Cognitive flexibility, Emotion regulation, agency and social intelligence
EF_Instrument: Semi-structured interviews (Levey et al 2016) (cognitive flexibility; emotion regulation; agency; social intelligence)
Justification_Resilience_conceptualizati: "Resilience was defined as evidence of adaptive functioning and psychological health. ...we will define resilience as evidence of daily functioning, ability to make realistic plans for the future, and presentation of an overall consistent and coherent narrative."
Comments_Relation_ACEs_EF_Resilience: "This study was undertaken in order to capture the needs of Liberian adolescents in their own words and identify the way forward. The goal of this research is to identify factors contributing to resilience among children in post-conflict Liberia. We will assess for the presence of these factors in the participants we interviewed and examine how they interact to promote resilience and adaptive functioning. Considering the findings in the literature reviewed and the observations made about resilience in children exposed to violence, we will define resilience as evidence of daily functioning, ability to make realistic plans for the future, and presentation of an overall consistent and coherent narrative."

Title: "Cognitive flexibility and perceived threat from COVID-19 mediante the relationships between Childhood mal treatment and state anxiety"
Affiliation_Corr_Author: "Psychology Department, Miami University, Oxford, Ohio, United States of America"
Research_Aim: "We examined the relations between adverse childhood experiences, assessed using the Adverse Childhood Experiences Scale (ACEs), perceived threat from COVID-19, and state anxiety in a sample of adults. Additionally, flexibility is implicated in adaptive coping with life’s stressors so we also assessed participants’ cognitive flexibility."
Research_Results: "Our data indicate that experience with early life adversity in the form of maltreatment is associated with increased perceived threat from COVID-19, which results in higher anxiety levels for the individual. In contrast, childhood maltreatment is associated with reduced flexibility in appraising challenges, which in turn mediates the relationship between maltreatment and anxiety. The findings of this study adds to the limited literature on the impact of early life adversity on cognitive flexibility and highlights the psychological toll of COVID-19 on individuals who have been exposed to adverse childhood experiences."
Population_Characteristics: White=80.1%; Asian=5.1%; Hispanic=5.9%; Africanamerican=6.5%; Native american=0.3%; Indianamerican=0.6%; Ethnicity_not_listed=0.6%; no_disclosure=0.3%
Specific_ACEs: emotional abuse; physical abuse; sexual abuse; physical neglect; emotional neglect; parents' separation or divorce; physical abuse; physical abuse threatening; family's substance abuse; family's serious illness; parents' jail
Specific_ACEs_Instruments: Adverse Childhood Experiences Scale [ACEs] (Felitti et al., 1998)
EF_Instrument: Cognitive Flexibility Inventory [CFI] (Dennis & Vander Wal 2010) (cognitive flexibility; cognitive control)
Justification_Resilience_conceptualizati: "Some individuals emerge from stressful life events with increased resilience whereas others develop psychopathologies (including depression and anxiety). This suggests the existence of individual level variability in response to life’s stressors. Considering that stressful life experiences are relatively commonplace, identifying factors that increase vulnerability to life’s stressors or confer resilience in stressful circumstances is essential. /// Psychologists have been interested in identifying factors that enhance an individual’s resilience in the face of stress. Fundamentally, the ability to bounce back from adversity requires adaptation to changing circumstances. Strategies to cope with stressful events must be flexibly applied to changing contextual demands. Cognitive flexibility is an aspect of flexibility. It is a multifaceted construct, exhibiting both trait and state characteristics, and a key component of executive functions. Although difficult to define, one definition of cognitive flexibility refers to the ability to switch flexibly between rules or shift between modes of thinking. In order to exhibit this form of cognitive flexibility, an individual must inhibit irrelevant information and deploy attention resources effectively. The ability to switch between set ways of thinking can be particularly useful when an individual confronts a stressor that they cannot control. /// Cognitive flexibility confers resilience. Cognitive flexibility may allow individuals to respond more adaptively to environmental stressors."
Comments_Relation_ACEs_EF_Resilience: "Childhood maltreatment is associated with reduced flexibility in appraising challenges. And with a reduced flexibility there is a weaker resilience. /// Our data show that experience with early life adversity in the form of maltreatment and household dysfunction was positively correlated with higher anxiety levels during a global pandemic. As such, individuals who reported one or more ACEs for maltreatment and household dysfunction were also more likely to report higher anxiety levels. /// In addition to perceived threat from COVID-19, our data demonstrated that exposure to maltreatment reduced the individual’s ability to flexibly appraise challenges, an aspect of cognitive flexibility measured by CFI-Control. This relation was also observed between household dysfunction and CFI-Control. /// Since CFI-Control is an indicator of the individual’s ability to flexibly view stressors as challenges (i.e. something within one’s control), our data suggests that early life adversity makes it more likely that an individual will view challenging circumstances in their daily life as threatening"

Title: "Elder Abuse and Cognitive Function among Community-Dwelling Older Adults: Does Abuse History Matter?"
Affiliation_Corr_Author: "Institute for Health, Health Care Policy and Aging Research, Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey, New Brunswick, New Jersey"
Research_Aim: "Examine the relationship between cumulative interpersonal violence and cognitive function"
Research_Results: "Older adults with EA (Elder Abuse) and abuse history (b=0.147, SE=0.052, p<.01) or abuse history only (b=0.118, SE=0.046, p<.01) had higher global cognition than the EA only group."
Population_Characteristics: Chinese; No Interpersonal Violence n=2,181; Abuse History Only n=310; EA (Elder Abuse) Only n=439 ; EA and Abuse History n=204
Specific_ACEs: physical abuse; insults; physical abuse threatening; screaming; curses; sexual abuse
Specific_ACEs_Instruments: 56-item modified Conflict Tactics Scale [CTS] (Straus et al., 1996); Unmet needs assessment (Moon et al., 2002); Financial Exploitation measure (Conrad et al., 2009); Extended Hurt Insult Threaten Scream scale [E-HITS] (Chan et al., 2010)
EF_Instrument: Mini-Mental State Examination [MMSE] (Folstein et al 1975) (global cognition); East Boston Story Test (Albert et al 1991) (episodic memory); Wechsler Memory Scale-Revised [DB] (Wechsler, 1987) (working memory); Symbol Digit Modalities Test [SDMT] (Smith 1982) (processing speed)
Justification_Resilience_conceptualizati: "The stress inoculation hypothesis indicates that adverse experiences may foster resilience,  manifested as a less negative health outcome when confronting subsequent stressors  (Meichenbaum, 1985). Exposure to the same stressor could reduce the subsequent impact  of the stressor through developing tolerance (Eysenck, 1983). Individuals may use their  past exposure to similar events to shift trauma from “outside the realm of an individual’s  experience” to the “normative” range of experiences that people deal with during their lives  (Norris & Murrell, 1988). Individuals might actually be more, rather than less, resilient to repeated exposures to trauma. On the other hand, sheltering from stressors may lead to a lack of toughness (Dienstbier, 1989)."
Comments_Relation_ACEs_EF_Resilience: Our findings reveals that abuse history makes older adults more silient in response to EA in later life, manifesting by better global cognition and cognitive domains(episodic memory, working memory, and proccessing speed). / The finding showed that older adults with EA (Elder Abuse) and abuse history had significantly higher global cognition, episodic memory, working memory, and processing speed than the EA-only group. Older adults with abuse history only had higher global cognition, episodic memory, and processing speed than the EAonly group. The relationship between interpersonal violence and cognitive function differs regarding different subtypes of abuse. / Our finding reveals that abuse history makes older adults more resilient in response to EA (Elder Abuse) in later life, manifesting by better global cognition and cognitive domains (episodic memory, working memory, and processing speed) even controlling medical comorbidities and depressive symptoms.

Title: "Executive functions in Palestinian Children: Effects of chronic conflict and psychosocial factors."
Affiliation_Corr_Author: "Université du Québec à Montréal (UQAM), Faculté des sciences de l’éducation, 1205 rue Saint-Denis, Montréal, Québec H2X 3R9, Canada"
Research_Aim: "The present study had three aims. First, its primary goal was to provide updated descriptive data on core executive functions in Palestinian children currently living in war-affected settings, thereby contributing to an underexplored area of research. Second, it aimed to compare the executive functioning of children living in two distinct regions—the Gaza Strip and the West Bank—which, while sharing several contextual similarities, differ in terms of the intensity and chronicity of exposure to traumatic events. Finally, from an exploratory perspective, the study examined potential associations between core executive functions, living regions and three psychosocial variables: perceived well-being, resilience, and the frequency of exposure to potentially traumatic events."
Research_Results: "Robust MANOVA indicated significant differences between groups, with Gaza children displaying slower but more accurate working memory performance and fewer reported traumatic events compared to their West Bank counterparts, who responded faster but with lower accuracy and reported higher trauma exposure. Within-group analyses revealed nuanced associations; higher resilience and well-being were linked to improved executive function outcomes, particularly in Gaza, highlighting potential protective effects. Conversely, trauma exposure exhibited context-specific cognitive correlates, suggesting differential impacts depending on trauma characteristics."
Population_Characteristics: Children enrolled in schools administered by the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees (UNRWA), residing in refugee camps in the West Bank (Jalazone, Shu’fat, Kalandia) and the Gaza Strip (Al-Shejayah, Al-Nusirat, Tall Al-Sultan).
Specific_ACEs: exposure to war-related violence; political violence; chronic armed conflict
Specific_ACEs_Instruments: Exposure to Potentially Traumatic Events Scale (Joma et al., 2021b)
Other_ACEs_Conceptualization: Exposure to potentially traumatic events related to war, political violence, and chronic conflict.
EF_Evaluated: Working memory; Inhibitory control; Cognitive flexibility
EF_Instrument: Stroop task (Stroop 1935) (inhibitory control); Spatial n-back task (Kirchner 1958) (working memory); Wisconsin Card Sorting Task [WCST] (Heaton et al 1993) (cognitive flexibility)
Justification_Resilience_conceptualizati: "Our data suggest that resilience, generally defined as the capacity to withstand and rebound from challenges, maintaining or quickly regaining mental health and functioning (Hall et al., 2022), may extend to cognitive performance: children who are able to psychologically adapt and find support."
Resilience_Instrument: Child and Youth Resilience Measure [CYRM] (Jefferies et al., 2019; Panter-Brick et al., 2018)
